Health Apps

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A timeous diagnosis can save your life. Carte Blanche looks at groundbreaking health Apps developed by local heroes to save and improve their patients' lives

Summary:
The country's largest private health insurance company, Discovery recently published global trends that show technology is driving rapid change in the way healthcare is delivered. In 2015 $4.5-billion of venture capital was invested in digital health businesses globally, to develop technology that not only improves diagnosis, but also patient monitoring; collecting health data to assist in improving health analytics. We introduce some of the local heroes behind the innovation stats, who are revolutionising health care through clever apps, and saving lives in deep-set rural, disadvantaged communities; the heroes that are addressing the difficulties health care workers face when they need specialist advice in a system that is generally lacking and slow. We show apps that give health workers new ways of helping their patients quick and efficient specialist care.

Further information:
The Vula App is designed for diagnostic assistance in Ophthalmology, Cardiology, Orthopaedics and Burns. The diagnostics that are used at the moment is in Ophthalmology. The rest of the diagnostics will be launched in 2 months. Vula is the brainchilld of Ophtalmologist and erstwhile rural doctor, Dr William Mapham. In 2010 a rock-climbing accident left Mapham considering the legacy he wished to leave, and he swapped Johannesburg for Swaziland to volunteer his TIME performing cataract surgery. Mapham's inspiration to develop the app came from WORKING in deep rural areas in Swaziland and the Eastern Cape where people had limited or no access to eye clinics. 'While conducting eye clinics in far-flung villages in the old Transkei I came across people who have been blind for many years and that needed cataract surgery to restore their vision. It was the obstacle of remoteness that Dr William Mapham, an ophthalmology registrar at Tygerberg hospital set out to overcome. Mapham "cold-called" an old University of Cape Town (UCT) peer, Shuttleworth Foundation fellow Mark Horner, for advice on funding. Mapham had to overcome some resistance from his peers. "Change management takes time," he says. Mapham previously spent time in New York and Washington where he designed mobile phone applications for healthcare.

The story will predominantly focus on Vula, but we will also briefly look at CrashDetech - a smartphone application, which automatically detects a serious car crash, pinpoints the location, immediately dispatches the nearest ambulance and supplies paramedics with lifesaving information. Crashdetech was developed by Jaco Gerrits, who has a technology background and was looking for a business with social impact. Gerrits won the 2007 top ICT Entrepreneur in SA Award. Gerrits believes in social entrepreneurship can change the world.

We will also show "The Triage Mobile App" which helps in assessing the degrees of urgency among waiting patients and deciding on the order of treatment for each of them. It is an effort to save more lives, reduce waiting time and improve efficiency in developing communities. The mobile app will help health practitioners by guiding them through the questions, vital signs and calculations used in triage process
We will also be looking at other locally developed Health assistance Apps and refer to them in the story

The final app we will show is government-developed "Mom Connect" -- where the Department of Health is registering every pregnant mother in SA to support the mother and baby during the course of the pregnancy up to child’s first birthday

PROMOS

10 secs Smart phone app technology has the potential to revolutionise the way doctors treat patients. Meet some South African visionaries who first spotted the health gaps that clever apps could fill. 

8 secs Could smart phone app technology reshape global healthcare, connecting doctors with remote patients?
7 secs WILL: thanks to technology and linking up with specialists, you really can offer your patients specialist care wherever you are…

5 secs In a country short of doctors, can health apps fill the gap?
10 secs NTENENG MOLEKA: It’s very difficult to describe a condition sometimes over the phone – so it’s so nice that one it able to take an image or take a video…within 10, 15 minutes I have an answer, solution and I know how to treat the patient.

Script:


INSERT
16secs In rural Porterville, Western Cape, community service doctor Nteneng Moleko is the only doctor on call to manage whomever and whatever conditions come through the door. But she’s not alone…Vula – Zulu for “open” – is an app that connects her with specialists at Tygerberg hospital.
NTENENG MOLEKA: VULA app is such an immense help to me – it’s very difficult to describe a condition sometimes over the phone – so it’s so nice that one it able to take an image or take a video…take a short history with it and then at the moment the doctor that I’m referring to can just sort of see exactly what I’m seeing – within 10, 15 minutes I have an answer, solution and I know how to treat the patient.
13 secs Tested on eyes, Vula’s growing into seven specialities – including orthopaedics, where surgeon Naas Terblanche says the app could even make virtual ward rounds possible once it’s been studied as all health apps should be.
DR NAAS TERBLANCHE: The Orthopaedics department under the auspices of the University of Stellenbosch will start doing some research to prove that the information that we get from the app is reliable and can be trusted.
JOHN WEBB: You’d be hard-pressed to find specialist treatment at most of the country’s rural hospitals – but now, thanks to the wonders of modern cell phone technology, our young doctors can carry specialists in their pockets.
38 secs Numerous studies show the rise of mobile medicine is reshaping global health. Health apps are among those most often downloaded. Research firm McKinsey predicts by 2020 one in four of us will use health apps – even now Americans are said to consult health apps before doctors…
One of the first health apps developed locally by doctor and television presenter Michael Mol was Hello Doctor. Registered doctors give advice through the app and sms, to make it more accessible – it’s now been bought by the MMI Health Group for their clients.
To remain the country’s largest medical aid, Discovery Health realised they had to lead app innovation too. Deputy CEO Ryan Noach.
DR RYAN NOACH: It can be extremely expensive – over 4 years we’ve invested more than a R150-million in our Health-ID development…I shouldn’t be age-discriminatory here, but are older than me and as a result haven’t worked much with apps and with tablets. And so we’ve been on a journey of teaching the doctors of how to use these tools.
9 secs Discovery’s HealthID app tracks their members’ activities in health form buying pills to hospital admissions, enabling doctors to see their whole big picture.
DR RYAN NOACH: We’ve been surprised by how difficult it is. Members and doctors see a simple app on the screen of the smart phone or tablet or even on the web, that really is just the front end…it’s like looking through the window into a massive complicated big factory in the background.
14 secs Without corporate big bucks, Tygerberg eye specialist in training Dr William Mapham dreamt of an app that could change the lot of state patients. Free, and dirt cheap to send lots of pictures and patient data, Vula is literally selling itself among his colleagues.
JOHN WEBB: You were always confident that it would work?
DR WILLIAM MAPHAM: I wouldn’t say that – I think, it was an idea…and with support became more than an idea…it became actually an obsession, I have to say. I spent a lot of time working on this – I would do my medical work during the day – go home – have supper with my wife, spend some time – when she went to bed I would work on vula, so for a long time I didn’t get that much sleep but I just couldn’t help it – I really just felt like I had to do this.
5 secs Will did community service in rural Eastern Cape, and volunteered at an eye clinic in Swaziland.
DR WILL MAPHAM: We had no support and you had to do the best you could do – I think I read more then than I did at medical school – but that was the source of our knowledge…whereas now, thanks to technology and linking up with specialists, you really can offer your patients specialist care wherever you are.
7 secs Will is fast becoming a tech fundi – but initially he was fobbed of by everyone except designer Debre Barrett.
DEBRE BARRETT: At the time we were getting at least once every two weeks one of those types of emails.
DR WILL MAPHAM: We had R50,000 and I thought it was enough to invent anything that you wanted to do in mobile technology…so I did have a few laughs when I approached other developers and they said look you can get one button for that – which button would you like? So I was very fortunate that Debre took me seriously and helped design the system.
DEBRE BARRETT: It’s a tool that enables you to refer the patients – so the patient is going to move to hospital and you just have to make sure that the patient is accepted at the destination but what we’re consistently seeing is that around 30% of all the referrals that come through he app just need advice so it takes the specialist often a minute to give that advice, it’s very very precious to the rural health care worker and it’s precious to the patient – instead of making a very difficult trip into the hospital they get treated on the spot.
3.5 secs Vula has won numerous tech awards that help fund its development.
DEBRE BARRETT: The reason why there’s a demand for Vula is because it fulfils a real need. And I think that’s the best kind of software – a piece of software that says there’s a need for this thing and nothing else is fulfilling that need.
22 secs With the mobile health market predicted to far exceed $30-billion by 2020, it’s no surprise social entrepreneurs like Jaco Gerrits seek out healthcare gaps like the public health threat of road fatalities and stretch app technology as far as it can go. The app detects a car crash and despatches emergency care, using sensors on smart phones.
JACO GERRITS: To develop a battery friendly algorithm that’s still consistent in terms of developing a life-saving service…that was technically quite a challenge for us. It’s the kind of app that you should have on your phone and just forget about it. We always say that you know what – we’ll know when you need us.
DR RYAN NOACH: The digitisation of the health care has enormous benefits – the primary benefit is of course improved quality of care.
